author: Irina Slav
excerpt: The Yemeni Houthis have struck Saudi Arabia’s southern province of Najran in the latest flare-up of Middle Eastern hostilities, killing 11 civilians, Reuters has reported, citing a spokesman for the military coalition led by Saudi Arabia that fights the Houthis in Yemen. The news comes on the heels
content:
The Yemeni Houthis have struck Saudi Arabia’s southern province of Najran in the latest flare-up of Middle Eastern hostilities, killing 11 civilians, Reuters has reported, citing a spokesman for the military coalition led by Saudi Arabia that fights the Houthis in Yemen.

The news comes on the heels of reports that Iran is considering a ban on U.S., Israeli, and other “hostile” vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and fining ships that violate the ban with a sum equal to 20% of the cargo’s value. From other vessels, Iran plans to ask for passage fees of between $5% and 7% of the cargo’s value.

The reports pushed oil prices higher today, with Brent crude recovering above $80 and trading at $83.80 per barrel at the time of writing. West Texas Intermediate also rebounded, trading at $78.33 per barrel earlier today.

In its report on the Houthi attacks, Reuters cited a senior Saudi official as saying the Houthis and Iran-affiliated Iraqi groups were planning to launch a coordinated attack on Saudi civilian targets, notably energy infrastructure and ports. This would further complicate the energy export situation in the Middle East as peace remains highly elusive.

The Houthis are also targeting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, with two vessels struck over the past week, lending additional support to oil prices. The Houthis themselves reported on Thursday an attack on Saudi troops in Yemen, which suggests that war is heating up yet again as well.

The latest events come after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier in the week said a deal was within reach and oil flows via Hormuz could resume as early as Wednesday. Instead of that happening, hostilities are escalating.

“Despite clear signs of progress in recent days, the tenor of the rhetoric and growing distrust between the US and Iran mean things could go from bad to worse once again,” ING commodity analysts wrote in a note earlier today.

By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

title: China’s Crude Imports Bounce Back After Historic June Slump
author: Irina Slav
excerpt: China’s crude oil imports reversed an earlier decline, rising by 22% from June to an average daily of 8.45 million barrels, or a total of 35.73 million tons, Bloomberg reported today, citing customs data. China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, culminating three months of
content:
China’s crude oil imports reversed an earlier decline, rising by 22% from June to an average daily of 8.45 million barrels, or a total of 35.73 million tons, Bloomberg reported today, citing customs data.

China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, culminating three months of very low import levels amid high prices and constrained supply from the Middle East. Beijing could afford to dramatically reduce its crude buying, slashing import volumes in June by an estimated 4.4 million barrels daily compared to the 2025 average.

The reason China was able to do that was that as of the end of 2025, the country held the world’s biggest stockpile of oil inventories at 1.397 billion barrels, according to estimates by the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That was more than the combined strategic inventories in the United States, Japan, OECD Europe, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, and India—the countries next down the list of the world’s top holders of strategic oil reserves.

Thanks to this substantial supply cushion, China became instrumental in keeping a cap on global oil prices despite the turmoil in the Middle East, as the biggest importer of the commodity in the world could hit pause on imports for a while. However, analysts warned earlier this year that at some point China will return to international markets and that would not be a good day for oil bears.

Earlier this week, a report by Reuters said that Sinopec, the world’s top refiner by capacity, has boosted purchases of Russia’s Far East crude for delivery in the third quarter as it looks to secure cargo arrivals amid continued shipping constraints in the Middle East.

State-run Sinopec has acquired as many as 30-40 shipments, or 241,000 to 320,000 barrels per day, of Russia's Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean (ESPO) for delivery between July and September.

title: Shipping Through Hormuz Drops Sharply as Tensions Rise
author: Tsvetana Paraskova
excerpt: Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has declined this week from the prior week amid uncertainty about the U.S.-Iran talks and the potential reopening of the Middle East’s key oil and LNG chokepoint. Between Monday and Thursday, a total of 33 vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz, down from
content:
Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has declined this week from the prior week amid uncertainty about the U.S.-Iran talks and the potential reopening of the Middle East’s key oil and LNG chokepoint.

Between Monday and Thursday, a total of 33 vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz, down from 50 for the same days last week, according to ship-tracking data monitored by Reuters.

On Thursday, as the market was expecting a draft Iran-Oman proposal for management of the Strait, four vessels moved through Hormuz, per Kpler data.

Only six crude oil tankers have managed to clear the Strait of Hormuz outbound so far this week, according to Kpler’s analysis cited by Reuters.

Vessel traffic at the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait crumbled earlier this week amid a Houthi claim they had hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea and hopes that Oman and Iran could reach a deal on jointly managing Hormuz.

Analysts at security and vessel-tracking firms told the BBC this week that the threats to shipping in the Gulf and the Red Sea have escalated to the worst safety situation since the Iran war began.

The market hopes of U.S.-Iran talks and an Iran-Oman deal on the management of the Strait of Hormuz appear to be dwindling at the end of this week.

Iran signaled a much more restrictive regime for vessel traffic than thought, with proposals under review at its parliament to ban U.S. and Israeli ships from transiting the Strait, while other nations that Tehran deems have harmed it would pay compensation for moving through Hormuz.

“Despite clear signs of progress in recent days, the tenor of the rhetoric and growing distrust between the US and Iran mean things could go from bad to worse once again,” ING’s commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note early on Friday.

In Friday trade in Asia, oil prices jumped with Brent Crude topping $83 per barrel, after the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen struck Saudi Arabia’s southern province of Najran in the latest flare-up of Middle Eastern hostilities, killing 11 civilians.  

By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

title: India Remains Dependent on Imports for 90% of Oil Demand
author: Tsvetana Paraskova
excerpt: Despite a decline in dependence on primary energy imports, India remains highly dependent, at a massive 90%, on crude oil imports for its consumption, a new industry report has shown. India’s dependence on primary energy imports fell to 42% in the financial year 2025 from 47% in FY 2017, according t
content:
Despite a decline in dependence on primary energy imports, India remains highly dependent, at a massive 90%, on crude oil imports for its consumption, a new industry report has shown.

India’s dependence on primary energy imports fell to 42% in the financial year 2025 from 47% in FY 2017, according to a joint report by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) and EY.

However, India remains highly dependent on crude oil imports, with 90% of all demand met by purchases from overseas, the report noted.

“Overall primary energy import dependence has reduced modestly from 47% to around 42% between FY17 and FY25, indicating gradual diversification of the energy system despite persistent dependence on imported oil,” media quoted the report as saying.

Set OilPrice.com as a preferred source in Google here.

India, the world’s third-largest crude oil importer, has seen its dependence on crude oil imports steadily rising in recent years amid soaring demand and falling domestic production.

The Middle East crisis sent Indian refiners scrambling for alternatives and the government looking to expand strategic storage sites to hold more reserves to cushion the next supply shocks.

India’s state-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), the top explorer in the country, will build a new storage site at Mangaluru to hold about 13 million barrels of oil.

In the wake of the Iran war and the disrupted crude flows at the Strait of Hormuz, India found itself in search of alternatives to replace the lost Middle Eastern supply. Record crude oil imports from Russia have helped cushion the blow, but India realized it needs additional storage sites to hold commercial and strategic reserves.

India is one of the biggest crude oil importers, but also one of the most exposed to supply shocks as its current maximum reserve capacity can cover only eight days of national oil demand.

Meanwhile, India’s state-run refiners continue their buying spree of crude from West Africa as the Middle East crisis has sapped supply and made deliveries uncertain.

By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

content:
By Editorial Dept - Aug 07, 2026, 6:30 AM CDT

September WTI crude oil futures are trading at $78.08 early Friday, down $8.72, or 10.05%, for the week. The market opened at $80.10, traded as high as $82.33, and fell to $74.24. With Friday’s session still ahead, the weekly result is not final. But the message from the price action is clear. Traders sold the possibility that diplomacy could restore crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz, then bought back part of the break when it became clear that the shipping problem had not been solved.

The early selloff was driven by optimism surrounding talks involving Iran, Oman and the United States. The market treated reports of progress as a path toward reopening Hormuz and releasing more Gulf crude into the global market. That was enough to pull a large amount of risk premium out of WTI in a short period.

The problem is that the market priced the result before it had the barrels. Iran wants influence over ships entering the Gulf and visibility over vessels leaving it. That may create a temporary arrangement, but it does not restore unrestricted shipping or give refiners confidence that cargoes will move on schedule.

WTI bounced from the weekly low, but the rebound did not erase the break. The market still believes a workable deal would reduce the supply risk. It is just no longer willing to assume that a diplomatic headline is the same as normal tanker traffic.

title: Gaza Ceasefire Unravels as Regional Pressure on Israel Grows
author: Editorial Dept
excerpt: Politics, Geopolitics & Conflict Eight Arab and Muslim countries have accused Israel of violating the Gaza ceasefire as Israeli strikes continue more than nine months after the U.S.-mediated “truce” took effect. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Egypt, Jordan, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia jointly cond
content:
By Editorial Dept - Aug 07, 2026, 6:30 AM CDT

Politics, Geopolitics & Conflict

Eight Arab and Muslim countries have accused Israel of violating the Gaza ceasefire as Israeli strikes continue more than nine months after the U.S.-mediated “truce” took effect. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Egypt, Jordan, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia jointly condemned Israeli attacks on civilians, healthcare facilities and other infrastructure. More than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the October ceasefire, according to Gaza health authorities. Israeli forces have also returned to areas from which they had agreed to withdraw, and humanitarian aid is languishing below levels required under the deal. Israel says Hamas has also violated the ceasefire by rebuilding tunnels, recruiting fighters and rearming, and has refused to complete its withdrawal until Hamas disarms. With the first phase having failed, the second phase - which calls for Hamas to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza - appears impossible.

Hezbollah has publicly offered talks with Syria for the first time, complicating U.S. efforts to draw Damascus into the effort to disarm the group. Hezbollah has intimated that it would have no problem meeting with the Syrian government. content:

Tehran would control inbound traffic while Oman would oversee outbound shipping, and Iran is seeking sanctions relief in exchange for toll-free passage. title: India's Crude Oil Output Falls for Third Straight Year
author: Tsvetana Paraskova
excerpt: India’s crude oil production fell for the third consecutive financial year in 2025/2026, the government said as it launches a push to boost offshore oil and gas exploration. India’s crude output fell by 3% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, Oil and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh
content:
India’s crude oil production fell for the third consecutive financial year in 2025/2026, the government said as it launches a push to boost offshore oil and gas exploration.

India’s crude output fell by 3% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, Oil and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri told Parliament.

“The domestic oil production over the last three years has shown a slight decline, primarily owing to natural decline in mature and ageing oil and gas fields,” the government said.

State-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), the biggest explorer in the country, contained the annual decline to about 2% thanks to Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) and Improved Oil Recovery (IOR).

Set OilPrice.com as a preferred source in Google here.

However, India aims to boost offshore oil and gas exploration to raise production and reduce dependence on imports, which is as much as 90% for crude oil.

Last month, the federal government launched the so-called National Offshore Exploration Scheme, with $8.8 billion in government support through FY 2030–31. The scheme is India’s most ambitious offshore exploration mission to date.

As part of the program, the government will provide financial support of up to 50% of the cost of drilling deepwater exploration wells. The support will reduce exploration risk, encourage investment, and accelerate the development of India's offshore hydrocarbon potential, according to the government.

India's future hydrocarbon potential lies largely in deepwater and ultra-deepwater basins such as Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Mahanadi, and the Andaman region. Exploration in these frontier areas requires advanced technology and significant investment, with a single deepwater exploratory well costing about $125–150 million.

“Recognising the high-risk, high-cost nature of such exploration, the Government is adopting a risk-sharing approach to encourage sustained investment, accelerate exploration, and unlock India's offshore hydrocarbon resources,” the federal government said.

As part of strengthening energy security, India also plans build new storage sites as the world’s third-largest crude oil importer looks to boost its resilience to supply shocks.

title: Senate Ag Committee Fails to Advance Farm Bill Over SNAP Dispute
author: Jesse Allen
excerpt: Senate Ag Committee Chariman John Boozman (R-AR) during Farm Bill markup on August 6th, 2026.(WASHINGTON D.C.) — The Senate Agriculture Committee’s markup of the Agricultural Act of 2026, known as “Farm Bill 2.0,” failed to advance Thursday
content:
Senate Ag Committee Chariman John Boozman (R-AR) during Farm Bill markup on August 6th, 2026.

(WASHINGTON D.C.) — The Senate Agriculture Committee’s markup of the Agricultural Act of 2026, known as “Farm Bill 2.0,” failed to advance Thursday on a 10-11 vote, leaving the bill in recess until Chairman John Boozman (R-AR) calls the committee back into session — likely in September, after the Senate returns from its August recess.

The vote broke down almost entirely along party lines, with most amendments decided 12-11 in Republicans’ favor. Twelve Republicans backed moving the bill out of committee, but Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) cast his vote by proxy while recovering from a fall, and Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-AL) left the room before the final vote — meaning that even with Tuberville present, the tally would have landed 11-11 and the bill still would have failed.

At the center of the impasse is a dispute over shifting SNAP benefit costs to states. Boozman said he negotiated directly with the White House to soften the bill’s nutrition provisions, agreeing to delay the state cost-sharing requirement by one year and to let states use whichever of their fiscal 2026 or 2027 SNAP payment error rates is lower to calculate future cost-sharing obligations. Democrats, led by Ranking Member Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), said that concession didn’t go far enough and pushed for a two-year delay instead, arguing a one-year window would let states with the highest error rates avoid cost-sharing longer than states that have already improved.

Sen. Ben Ray Lujan (D-NM) offered an amendment extending the delay by an additional year, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would cost roughly $19 billion. It failed on a party-line vote, as did most of the 13 amendments Democrats introduced. The markup had anticipated as many as 206 amendments, but with talks largely stalled over SNAP, most Republican priorities were instead folded into a 34-amendment manager’s package that passed as part of the bill.

“We’re not going to get a farm bill. That’s the game here today,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) earlier in the hearing. “All of us knew before we walked in this room. This is going to fall to a partisan vote over SNAP payments.”

Country-of-Origin Labeling Passes, Other Amendments Added

One of the markup’s few bipartisan moments came on mandatory country-of-origin labeling (MCOOL) for beef, which passed 17-6 despite a bipartisan split within the GOP itself. Six Republicans — including Boozman — voted against the amendment even though it was led by Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). Sens. Deb Fischer, John Hoeven, Cindy Hyde-Smith, Chuck Grassley and Joni Ernst joined Thune in support, while McConnell, Roger Marshall, Tuberville, Jim Justice and Jerry Moran voted no alongside Boozman. All committee Democrats backed the amendment. MCOOL is supported by the U.S. Cattlemen’s Association and R-CALF USA, and opposed by the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association.

The committee also debated but did not adopt proposals to restore roughly $2 billion in cuts to the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP) and to require audits of Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) payments. Sen. Peter Welch (D-VT), who offered the ARC audit amendment, argued the same scrutiny applied to SNAP wasn’t being applied to farm payment programs. Grassley, who noted he’s worked on seven farm bills, said he agreed with the amendment’s underlying intent but voted against it anyway, telling Welch, “I can’t vote for your bill,” as the committee remained split along party lines.

Other provisions that were folded into the bill via the manager’s package include permanently moving the Food for Peace program to USDA, funding for local food procurement programs, reauthorization of a cost-share grant program under the Roll-Over Prevention and Safety (ROPS) Act for retrofitting older tractors with rollbars, allowing hot rotisserie chicken purchases through SNAP, and year-round, nationwide sales of E15 — a priority corn-state lawmakers in both parties have pushed for years.

What’s Next

Boozman said he can reconvene the committee later this year as negotiations continue. With the Senate now headed into its August recess and midterm campaigning ahead, timing will be the key thing to watch — DTN reporting indicates the committee is expected to return to the table in September. Below you will find various statements from lawmakers and ag organizations after Thursday’s Senate Ag Committee meeting:

Republican Statements

Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman (R-AR)

“I’m deeply disappointed by this outcome. We have a responsibility to stand with America’s farmers, ranchers and rural communities. Everyone recognizes the serious challenges they continue to face, and blocking the farm bill only adds to the uncertainty and hardship.” Boozman added that “Democrats remain fixated on a partisan policy that allows states to continue the incredible wasteful spending of taxpayer dollars, ignoring our negotiated proposal. This debate was about the FARM BILL, not protecting the mismanagement of billions of dollars in food aid.”

“This legislation was crafted to earn broad support and incorporated more than 100 bipartisan bills and priorities, including authorizing year-round sales of E15, while addressing the real needs of our producers and rural communities who depend on it. America’s farmers and ranchers have pleaded for more farm in the farm bill. Republicans provided it and Democrats rejected it and they simply cannot afford continued delays. The status quo is not only unsustainable for farm country. It is catastrophic. They deserve the certainty, stability and support only a bipartisan farm bill can provide.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD)

“Democrats’ refusal to support the farm bill and year-round E15 is deeply disappointing and only creates more uncertainty for South Dakota’s farmers and ranchers. This bill includes over 100 bipartisan bills, yet Democrats chose to put partisan politics above producers and rural America. I know Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee stand ready to enact these sensible agriculture policies.”

Senator John Hoeven (R-ND)

“Farm Bill 2.0 is focused on supporting family farms and ranches and providing the tools and resources they need to succeed. The legislation improves the farm safety net, advances ag research and develops better market access for producers. Given the challenges in farm country, our producers need long-term certainty, and this legislation includes more than 100 bipartisan proposals to address real issues facing U.S. producers, including enhancements to the farm safety net, increased access to credit, year-round sale of E15, and many others. We’ll continue working with our colleagues to find a path forward for the Farm Bill.”

Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA)

“I’m very disappointed Democrats blocked the Farm Bill today in protest over commonsense reforms that root out waste in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and protect the integrity of the SNAP program. Democrats’ obstruction leaves the fate of the Farm Bill in serious jeopardy at a time when farmers need our help. I’ve fought tooth and nail for years to deliver a new, five-year Farm Bill and nationwide, year-round E15 for Iowa’s family farmers, and I’m not done working toward that goal. Rural America is counting on us.”

“Farmers don’t throw in the towel when the going gets tough, and Democrats shouldn’t either. It’s up to Democrats to put politics aside, engage in good faith negotiations and accept bipartisan compromise in order to get the Farm Bill passed in the Senate this year. I’m hopeful the committee can improve the bill and vote again when the Senate returns in September to achieve a more positive outcome.”

Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE)

“It is disgraceful Democrats refused to advance the bipartisan Farm Bill out of committee. First, Senate Democrats refused to stand up for our service members by not moving the bipartisan NDAA. Now, they’re turning their backs on farmers, ranchers, and rural America. We worked with them to secure bipartisan support for E15 and offered a compromise on SNAP cost share concerns. What did the Democrats do? They voted against every policy they claim to care about: funding food banks, improving rural and mental health services, increasing access to safe drinking water, and expanded broadband connectivity. This is a massive disservice to producers and communities across the country. I certainly hope they wake up and realize the pain this will inflict on American families.”

Senator Roger Marshall (R-KS), on RFD-TV

“Well, this is horribly disappointing — the Democrats just voted down the Farm Bill on the Senate Ag Committee. You know, I think the shocking part is they walked away from year-round E15, they walked away from five years of certainty when it comes to crop protection programs. So, we raised the reference prices 10% to 20% in the Working Families Tax Cuts bill, and this would have given folks five years of certainty. It raised the loan limits from USDA, it had more high-speed internet for rural America, and infrastructure, and farmer mental health — all those things. And they walked away from it because of an error rate issue when it comes to SNAP programs. And you know, happy to dive into that, but that’s really what their only hangup is. This bill is full of bipartisan priorities, but they’re hung up on the fact that we want states to be accountable — that if they have a high error rate on administering SNAP, then the states would have to pay more, or some fair share, of those SNAP benefits. So it’s just horrible news for the American farmer and rancher.”

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-MS)

“We were given a choice to move forward with a strong bipartisan compromise that serves the best interests of American farmers, ranchers and rural communities or to continue clinging to insincere lip service that does nothing to help anyone. I’m disappointed that Farm Bill 2.0 was stopped today because this was our chance to deliver the certainty and support that farmers and ranchers in Mississippi and across the nation not only deserve but need to compete and prosper in today’s marketplace. Despite the committee being at loggerheads today, I will continue to work with Chairman John Boozman and my colleagues to get a new farm bill over the finish line this year.”

House Agriculture Committee Chairman Glenn “GT” Thompson

“On behalf of our nation’s farmers, ranchers, and rural Americans, I am deeply disappointed in the results of today’s farm bill markup in the Senate Agriculture Committee. It is clear that Senate Democrats are not in search of real solutions for farm country. Even the inclusion of year-round E15, dozens of Democrat amendments, and a delay in the SNAP benefit cost share could not entice Senate Democrats to support producers and vote for the farm bill. Chairman Boozman and his team went above and beyond to accommodate requests from across the aisle, even including some compromises that we are not fully comfortable with in the House. Despite this, Democrats could not get to a yes.”

Democratic Statements

Ranking Member Amy Klobuchar (D-MN)

“I want us to get to a bipartisan agreement. But first and foremost, that includes addressing this ridiculous SNAP situation.”

On the White House’s spending priorities elsewhere: “If somehow the White House can find $70 billion extra for ICE, and they can ask for $70 billion for Iran, we can fix this second year.”

On the inequity created by a one-year delay: “What we are asking for is simply to not have a situation where one state that has double the error rate of my home state is able to get off scot-free for two years.”

“I am committed to continuing to work with Chairman Boozman on this bill to get it done and there are good things in it for our farmers and ranchers, including year-round E-15, a provision I have long led on. As noted by the Chairman, the Agriculture Committee meeting remains open for further discussions on this bill. Today we also included a package of additional bipartisan amendments that I voted for and have long supported. I also appreciate that the Chairman has acknowledged the problem with the SNAP cost shift to states and counties. But amid tariff-related rising grocery prices in states across the country where SNAP has been critical, this is only a one-year fix. It still advantages high error rate states over states with mid-level error rates. A state with an error rate twice that of Minnesota will pay nothing in the second year, whereas states that have reduced their error rates will still be disadvantaged over high error rate states. Our members are simply asking for the two-year delay so all states will be on the same footing in working to reduce their error rates. That is ten percent of the total SNAP cuts.”

Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ)

“We’re not going to get a farm bill. That’s the game here today. All of us knew before we walked in this room. This is going to fall to a partisan vote over SNAP payments.”

Senator Ben Ray Lujan (D-NM)

On his amendment to extend the SNAP cost-share delay: “Causing more hunger in America is simply shameful.”

Senator Peter Welch (D-VT)

“Senate Republicans’ Farm Bill failed to meet the moment. I’m hopeful we can come to the table in good faith to make substantial changes to this Farm Bill, and work together in a bipartisan way to make a real difference for rural America.”

On applying the same scrutiny to farm payments as SNAP: “The same principle that we’re applying to the SNAP program may not have been applied to the payment programs.”

Senator Tina Smith (D-MN)

“Patience is a virtue, it’s just not my virtue. I’m disappointed that we could not come to agreement on the Senate Farm Bill today, but we will keep working to find a path forward. It’s crucial that we pass a bipartisan Farm Bill that meets the needs of farmers, ranchers and rural America, including year-round E15.”

“I’m glad that several of my provisions are included in this bill. However, it is not possible to pass a Farm Bill that fails to fix the deep cuts to SNAP that are taking food off the table for millions of Americans, including at least 1.5 million children. Democrats have offered a commonsense solution that would delay the giant cost shift to county taxpayers, which would end up costing Minnesota taxpayers $140 million, for two years. While the Republicans have not accepted this so far, we will keep working. I’m grateful for the relentless efforts of Ranking Member Klobuchar to improve this Farm Bill and find a bipartisan solution. Amid shrinking markets, tariffs and skyrocketing costs for fuel and fertilizer caused by Trump’s war in Iran, farmers need Congress to get the job done.”

Ag Industry & Organization Statements

NCGA President Jed Bower

“We are extremely disappointed that legislation important to so many Americans failed to advance. This bill was particularly important to corn growers who have long pushed for legislation that would allow for the year-round sale of E15, a bright spot in an otherwise dim economic outlook. We implore senators to approve a bipartisan farm bill that extends consumer access to E15 and serves the interests of America’s farmers. We are running out of time in this Congress and urge action as quickly as possible.”

American Soybean Association

The American Soybean Association is disappointed that the Agricultural Act of 2026 was not advanced during today’s markup by the Senate Agriculture Committee. While the legislation was tabled for further consideration, today’s action delays much-needed progress toward enacting a bipartisan five-year farm bill. America’s soybean farmers continue to face a challenging farm economy marked by rising input costs, low commodity prices, and ongoing trade uncertainty. ASA urges lawmakers to use the August recess to continue bipartisan negotiations, engage directly with farmers and agricultural stakeholders, and resolve the remaining issues preventing the bill from moving forward. The Senate should return in September prepared to advance a comprehensive five-year farm bill and deliver the certainty and support America’s farmers need.

National Council of Farmer Cooperatives President and CEO Duane Simpson

“We are deeply disappointed that the Senate Agriculture Committee was unable to advance the Agricultural Act of 2026. This is a critical setback for the farmers, ranchers, co-ops, and rural communities who have waited far too long for meaningful relief. American agriculture is already under extreme economic strain while producers must use programs that have not been updated since 2018. Our nation’s farm families, along with the American consumers who depend on a safe and reliable food supply, cannot go another year without the certainty they urgently need. We urge the Senate Agriculture Committee to find a path forward for agricultural producers and Americans without further delay.”

National Association of Wheat Growers (NAWG)

Following the markup, NAWG called on committee leaders to quickly resume bipartisan negotiations and reconvene to advance a comprehensive farm bill. Although the legislation did not advance, the committee adopted several important agricultural priorities, including language permanently transferring the Food for Peace program to USDA. NAWG appreciates the work undertaken by committee members and urges lawmakers to build on that progress rather than allow the process to stall. Wheat growers need the certainty of an updated farm safety net as farmers continue to face significant economic pressure. NAWG will remain engaged with lawmakers to support passage of a bipartisan farm bill and additional economic and disaster assistance.

National Sorghum Producers Chair Amy France

“We are disappointed that the committee failed to advance legislation important to farmers and rural America. Especially at a time when producers are facing weak prices, high costs and continued uncertainty. We urge senators in both parties to return to the table as soon as possible. Congress needs to deliver a bipartisan farm bill that provides farmers certainty, expands markets through year-round E15 and preserves Sen. Moran’s Food for Peace amendment.”

National Pork Producers Council President Rob Brenneman

“When Congress passes a new farm bill, it must include the ask of America’s 60,000-plus pork producers to finally stop the threat of a state-by-state patchwork of farm animal housing laws spurred by California Proposition 12. America’s pork producers deserve a robust farm bill, which should come with protection from being forced to rebuild their barns every time another state decides it knows what is best for animal welfare over farmers. Not only does Prop. 12 make sustaining their businesses onerous for pork producers, but also it hinders the critical input and expertise of swine veterinarians.”

National Farmers Union President Rob Larew

“Family farmers can’t afford more delay, so it’s disappointing that the Senate Agriculture Committee did not come to an agreement on the farm bill. Family farmers and ranchers need the right farm bill – one that addresses today’s challenges and anticipates future needs. That means a farm safety net that accounts for high input costs and persistently low prices, along with stronger conservation funding and real protections against corporate monopolies. We saw some encouraging signs of bipartisanship through this process. The committee voted overwhelmingly to reinstate mandatory country-of-origin labeling and adopted an amendment funding local food procurement programs. The bill also included year-round, nationwide sale of E15, a change that will benefit both farmers and consumers.”

“It is essential that lawmakers work together to get a strong farm bill signed into law. Congress is running out of time to get this done. In the weeks ahead, Farmers Union members will continue pushing for farm and food policy improvements to help everyone in our communities.”

R-CALF USA CEO Bill Bullard

“Today’s vote marks the most significant step toward restoring mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef in more than a decade and demonstrates the broad bipartisan support for this issue. We thank Senate Majority Leader John Thune for his leadership in advancing this amendment and the bipartisan group of senators who supported it. We also recognize the thousands of independent cattle producers and consumers who have remained committed to this effort for many years.”

Invest In Our Land Executive Director Rebecca Bartels

“Farmers and ranchers need a Farm Bill, and they need one that gets conservation right. We appreciate the work Chairman Boozman and members on both sides of the aisle have put into this process, and we recognize the durable support many members of this Committee have shown for conservation over the years. We also want to thank Ranking Member Klobuchar and Senator Bennet for offering amendments that would have protected the Environmental Quality Incentives Program and the Conservation Stewardship Program from proposed reductions. Those amendments identified the right problem, and we hope the Committee uses this time to solve it. This is an opportunity, not a setback. We welcome further negotiation on EQIP and stand ready to work with members in both parties on a Conservation Title that protects the long-term commitment Congress made to working lands conservation just last year.”

International Fresh Produce Association (IFPA)

“America’s fruit and vegetable growers need the certainty that only a strong, bipartisan five-year Farm Bill can provide. The markup highlighted both progress and unfinished work on key specialty crop priorities, including the need to strengthen the Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework. IFPA remains committed to working with Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle to advance legislation that further invests in the long-term resilience of specialty crop growers and helps Americans put more fruits and vegetables at the center of a healthy diet.”

Specialty Crop Farm Bill Alliance (SCFBA)

“The Specialty Crop Farm Bill Alliance is grateful to Chairman Boozman for convening today’s markup and for including in his manager’s package an amendment offered by Sen. Schiff to protect the integrity of the definition of specialty crops in USDA programs and services. We are also grateful to Sen. Lujan for filing an amendment to make the Specialty Crop Emergency Framework mandatory and Sen. Slotkin for filing an amendment to enhance the Federal Crop Insurance Program for specialty crop producers, which is also supported by the Crop Insurance and Reinsurance Bureau. We look forward to working with members of the Senate Agriculture Committee to add the Lujan and Slotkin amendments to the farm bill as the legislative process continues. Despite today’s setback, we remain hopeful the Senate can find a bipartisan path forward to pass the Agriculture Act of 2026.”

Farm Credit Council President and CEO Christy Seyfert

“Farm Credit thanks Chairman Boozman, Ranking Member Klobuchar and the Senate Agriculture Committee for their efforts to advance a Farm Bill 2.0. Though we are disappointed that the committee could not successfully pass the Agriculture Act of 2026 today, we support the Chairman and Ranking Member in their commitment to continue negotiating over the in-state work period. As producers navigate ongoing economic uncertainty, completing a five-year Farm Bill is more important than ever. The Farm Bill includes bipartisan provisions to increase credit availability for farmers and ranchers, strengthen crop insurance, and modernize Farm Service Agency (FSA) loans and programs. We remain committed to working with members on both sides of the aisle to advance a complete, five-year Farm Bill this year to provide certainty for rural America.”

International Dairy Foods Association President and CEO Michael Dykes, D.V.M.

“IDFA supports the draft Farm Bill brought forth by Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Boozman and appreciates his determination to craft a bipartisan Farm Bill. IDFA is disappointed that the Senate Agriculture Committee was unable to advance the Farm Bill legislation today, delaying action on policies that would benefit American families, farmers, food manufacturers and rural communities.”

“The bill contained several important dairy priorities, including expansion of the Dairy Nutrition Incentive Program (DNIP), which would help more SNAP participants access nutrient-dense dairy foods such as milk, cheese and yogurt while supporting healthier American diets, permanent authorization of Mandatory Cost Surveys and the Dairy Forward Pricing Program, a manager’s amendment that was adopted containing the Codifying Useful Regulatory Definitions Act (CURD Act) and permanently transferring the Food for Peace program to USDA, and much-needed certainty for dairy farmers and the broader agricultural sector through a five-year Farm Bill.”

“IDFA remains committed to working with Chairman Boozman, all members of the Committee and the Administration to advance a bipartisan five-year Farm Bill that supports nutrition, strengthens the dairy industry and ensures families across the country have access to wholesome, nutritious dairy foods which they rely on each and every day. It is imperative that the U.S. Senate continues discussions to advance a long-term Farm Bill before the end of this Congress.”

Defeat EATS Coalition

“The Save Our Bacon Act presents a serious threat to American agriculture. Its passage would further tilt the scales towards industrial agriculture, eliminate important markets for independent farmers, limit consumer access to products they demand, and override hundreds of animal protection and public health and safety laws. The Defeat EATS coalition applauds the continued exclusion of this dangerous poison pill from the Farm Bill. It is clear that a bipartisan Farm Bill cannot pass the Senate if it includes the Save Our Bacon Act.”

State & Regional Reaction

North Dakota Farmers Union President Matt Perdue

“Family farmers and ranchers have been advocating to get a farm bill done for three years now. Over that time, economic conditions have worsened, input costs have gone up, and commodity demand has become increasingly uncertain. Despite those deepening challenges, farm policy continues to be mired in partisan gridlock. We appreciate all the work that has gone into this bill. But the plain reality is farm bills don’t pass the U.S. Senate without bipartisan support. We urge the Senate Agriculture Committee to find common ground on programs that support our hungry neighbors. The stakes are too high to walk away now.”

Minnesota Farm Bureau President Dan Glessing

“While Minnesota Farm Bureau appreciates Senators Klobuchar and Boozman’s continued leadership on the farm bill, today’s setback is a disappointment. The bill included several provisions our members advocated for, including year-round E-15, but not moving it forward today sets up farmers for continued unpredictability. This has been a priority for our members for over three years, and to see it pushed down the road again is frustrating. We urge the committee to come together and pass this important legislation.”

Illinois Soybean Growers

Illinois Soybean Growers (ISG) is disheartened that the Senate Agriculture Committee did not advance the Agricultural Act of 2026 today. Illinois soybean farmers need the stability that comes with a bipartisan, five-year Farm Bill, and today’s outcome further delays much-needed progress. Farmers continue to face tight margins, rising input costs and market uncertainty, making passage of a comprehensive bill critical to the future of agriculture.

With the last Farm Bill enacted in 2018, farmers have waited years for an updated framework that provides the long-term stability they need to make decisions and plan ahead. ISG urges Congress to continue working toward a bipartisan solution and return from the August recess prepared to advance a Farm Bill that gives farmers the confidence and tools they need to remain competitive.

Iowa Farmers Union President Aaron Lehman

“Farmers need a strong farm bill now more than ever. With markets suffering from dysfunctional tariffs, farm input prices increasing due to monopolies and wars without victory in sight, and food insecurity issues rising throughout Iowa, it is clear that now is the time to act. Historically, farm bills have been an investment in farmers, ranchers, and rural communities as well as in nutrition programs for all Americans. Without those investments from Congress, it means farmers and rural Iowans won’t be able to deliver the solutions from the farm when we need them the most.”

“This farm bill is three years overdue, and now time is running out to get the job done. Farmers don’t have the option to walk away from their fields and pastures if the job isn’t done. Congress should learn from that lesson and come together with solutions instead of walking away from their work.”

title: The Value of Official Identification Ear Tags
author: Susan Littlefield
excerpt: A Note from American Sheep Industry’s Animal Health Committee Co-Chairs As sheep producers, we are responsible for officially identifying cull ewes and rams, breeding stock of all ages being sold, sheep going to shows, and, in some
content:
A Note from American Sheep Industry’s Animal Health Committee Co-Chairs

As sheep producers, we are responsible for officially identifying cull ewes and rams, breeding stock of all ages being sold, sheep going to shows, and, in some states, lambs sold through auction markets. Requirements vary depending on the animal and state regulations, but official identification remains an important part of protecting our industry’s markets. This requirement has been in place since 2001, when the National Scrapie Eradication Program was launched. Although most of the industry follows these regulations, there is still room to improve compliance. Recent events highlight why official ID is so important.

With New World Screwworm (NWS) detections affecting animal movement, states without NWS cases are requiring and inspecting official identification on sheep moving from affected states. These states are working to protect their livestock industries by verifying where incoming animals originate. In addition, the recent detection of scrapie in ewe at a slaughter facility in Oregon through routine slaughter surveillance is a reminder that disease traceability is essential. Official USDA-approved ear tags are available in several types, and the costs are quite reasonable.

Tags can be applied at any point in an animal’s life. Some operations find it easiest to tag lambs at birth and use those tags for management purposes, while others tag sheep in chutes or trailers as animals leave the ranch of origin. Sheep may also be tagged at auction markets. Official identification, along with producer and sale records, help keep market channels open for our industry giving animal health officials the ability to respond quickly when disease is detected while minimizing disruptions to producers. We should be proud of these efforts because they have helped protect our industry and will continue to do so in the future.

title: ADNOC Buys 11 Supertankers for $1.3 Billion to Expand Export Fleet
author: Michael Kern
excerpt: ADNOC has bought 11 very large crude and gas carriers for $1.3 billion as the national oil company of Abu Dhabi continues to expand its fleet of supertankers to boost crude and LNG exports. ADNOC’s unit ADNOC Logistics & Services plc on Friday announced it had acquired five modern Very Large Gas Car
content:
ADNOC has bought 11 very large crude and gas carriers for $1.3 billion as the national oil company of Abu Dhabi continues to expand its fleet of supertankers to boost crude and LNG exports.

ADNOC’s unit ADNOC Logistics & Services plc on Friday announced it had acquired five modern Very Large Gas Carriers (VLGCs) and six Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) for a combined investment of about $1.3 billion.

Nine of the vessels, six VLCCs and three VLGCs, were acquired on the secondary market. They are scheduled for delivery this quarter and will enter service with ADNOC immediately following delivery.

The remaining two VLGCs are newbuild vessels acquired through a resale transaction from a Chinese shipyard, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026.

The fleet expansion will support ADNOC L&S’ gas and crude oil shipping capacity and support ADNOC Group’s integrated value chain and continued growth in production, trading and export volumes, the company said in a statement.

The latest acquisition follows ADNOC’s order for newbuild LNG carriers from last month.

ADNOC L&S currently owns over 340 vessels and operates 600 chartered ships.

The UAE has sought to adapt to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by sneaking tankers in dark mode through the Strait and increasingly offering to sell many of its crude grades for loading offshore Fujairah and at Sohar in Oman, outside the Strait.

The United Arab Emirates has managed to boost its oil exports to pre-crisis levels as early as June, as it has kept pushing crude through the Strait of Hormuz and outside it.

ADNOC is also boosting its LNG carrier fleet to grow its international gas business.

Last month, ADNOC Logistics and Services placed a $900-million order for four newbuild LNG carriers to expand its fleet as Abu Dhabi’s national oil company seeks to boost gas exports to capitalize on the global rise in LNG demand.

By Michael Kern for Oilprice.com

title: Ukraine Faces a Growing Air Defense Crisis as Patriot Supplies Dwindle
author: RFE/RL staff
excerpt: Ukraine's failure to intercept a single Russian missile during a large-scale overnight attack this week has raised fresh concerns over Kyiv's dwindling supply of air-defense interceptors as Moscow escalates its ballistic missile strikes on the nearly defenseless capital and other regions. Ukrainian
content:
Ukraine's failure to intercept a single Russian missile during a large-scale overnight attack this week has raised fresh concerns over Kyiv's dwindling supply of air-defense interceptors as Moscow escalates its ballistic missile strikes on the nearly defenseless capital and other regions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that deliveries of anti-ballistic interceptor missiles from partner countries have fallen sharply, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to deadly attacks that are being launched by Russia with increasing frequency.

Following a meeting with Ukraine's military leadership on protecting critical infrastructure on August 2, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had received only a third as many air-defense interceptors this year compared to the same period in 2025.

"Our partners have the missiles. What is needed are the necessary political decisions on deliveries and on accelerating production, including localization in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.

Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze, who was in Kyiv during the most recent attack on August 5, condemned Russia's latest strikes, which lit up the late-night skies with balls of flames from massive explosions.

"It was a vile attack on Ukrainians. I was hiding in the shelter along with a number of them and admiring their resilience. Russia is a terrorist state and needs to be contained," she wrote on X.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha also urged allies not to slow military assistance.

Speaking on August 5, he said: "Russian strikes take no summer vacation; support for Ukraine and pressure on the aggressor must not pause, either. Every interceptor counts. They are life-saving tools."

US Stockpile Questions

Patriot interceptor missiles remain Ukraine's most effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles, but questions are growing over how many additional interceptors Washington can realistically provide.

Last week, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated that the United States has used more than half of its Patriot PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptor inventories during its military operations against Iran this year.

The report estimated that US stocks of Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors have fallen from more than 2,300 before the conflict, which began in February, to roughly 800, while THAAD interceptor inventories have been nearly halved.

Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with CSIS and co-author of the report, told RFE/RL that the shortages leave Washington with little flexibility to supply Ukraine.

"Ukraine will not be able to expect many interceptors -- or any interceptors -- from the United States for quite a while," Cancian said. "The US has used extensively its own inventories.... We're down to about 800 or 900 [Patriot interceptors]. The war planners don't want to go below that, so it would be very difficult to provide any of those or any new production to Ukraine.”

Cancian said Ukraine may instead have to seek Soviet-designed S-300 missiles from countries that still operate the system and intensify efforts to destroy Russian missile launchers before they can fire.

His assessment contrasts with public assurances from the Trump administration.

CNN, citing unnamed officials, reported on August 4 that Patriot inventories had fallen to "dangerously low" levels. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected that report, calling it "fake news."

Just days earlier, the Pentagon announced agreements with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman to expand production of Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD interceptors.

US President Donald Trump insisted early on August 6 that the United States has "massive" amounts of munitions.

Trump also had pledged to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot missile interceptors, only to appear to backtrack on that promise days later.

"Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.

"The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" he added.

However, US administration officials who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity said the CSIS estimates broadly reflect the current state of American interceptor inventories.

Cancian said rebuilding those stockpiles will take years despite efforts to accelerate production.

"The United States is expanding production," he said. "Before the war in Ukraine, it was producing about 300 Patriot interceptors a year. Now we're up to about 600. We're trying to get to 2,000 a year, but that will take until at least 2030."

Even then, he said, Ukraine will have to compete with other US partners for new production.

"The Gulf states have used a lot of their Patriots [in the current Gulf conflict]. They want their inventories replenished, so there'll be a lot of competition for the new production. It may be four or five years before supply meets demand."

Risks For Ukraine

The prospect of fewer US interceptors raises immediate questions for Ukraine as Russia steps up missile attacks ahead of another winter.

Adding to the urgency, several media reports, including from Reuters, quoted Ukrainian military intelligence sources as saying a North Korean missile unit had begun deploying to western Russia and ‌could be equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for attacks on Ukraine.

Kervin Aucoin, a US Army veteran and former military intelligence analyst, said reduced US inventories will inevitably affect Kyiv.

"It's not going to be none, but it will be far less than what Ukraine was expecting," Aucoin told RFE/RL.

Still, he argued that Ukraine has repeatedly adapted to changing battlefield conditions.

"Ukraine is doing a great job…. If they can't rely on the US, unfortunately, they will rely on their own resilience, and they will continue to succeed on the battlefield," he said.

Over time, he said, Ukraine may increasingly turn toward cheaper technologies, including drone-based air defense and laser systems, rather than relying primarily on costly Patriot interceptors.

Republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee, told RFE/RL he believes the White House remains committed to supporting Ukraine.

"When I talk to people in the White House, they are absolutely committed to supporting Ukraine. I'm confident they will provide Ukraine with the weapons it needs when it needs them."

Cancian also warned that depleted US inventories could influence how America's adversaries assess Washington's military readiness.

"China is what the United States is most worried about," he told RFE/RL. "Using so many interceptors has created a window of vulnerability, and China might try to take advantage of that."

He added that Iran could reach similar conclusions: "Iran is certainly looking at this and thinking that the United States might be unwilling to recommence hostilities because of these growing shortages."

Ukraine Looks To Europe

With US supplies under pressure, Ukraine is increasingly looking to European allies.

US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker recently said Washington is exploring joint production of Patriot interceptors with Ukraine and European partners.

He stressed, though, that the immediate priority is to provide Ukraine with the air defense capabilities it needs to survive another winter, either from allies with excess interceptors or through increased production at US factories.

Kyiv has already begun that effort.

In early July, then-Defense Minister Mykhaylo Fedorov sent requests to nearly 40 countries seeking the temporary transfer of Patriot interceptors from existing inventories, proposing to replace them later with missiles from future production.

Ukraine has not disclosed which countries received the requests.

Within the European Union, a key provider of military assistance to Ukraine, seven countries operate Patriot systems: Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Spain, and Romania.

RFE/RL asked those governments on August 5 whether they would consider supplying additional interceptors following Ukraine's failure to intercept any Russian missiles during the overnight attack.

Germany declined to comment on operational matters, as did Romania, which called it a "matter of national security."

Sweden pointed to its contribution of an additional $108 million to the PURL initiative, bringing its total support for the program to $535 million.

The Netherlands has previously said it has already donated everything it could spare from its own Patriot inventories, and is providing Ukraine with around 3 billion euros per year in military aid until at least 2029.

"We have already delivered Patriots missiles and are currently unable to deliver more missiles from our existing stockpiles. At the same time, we are open to exploring any option that helps Ukraine protect its skies and people. Air defense has been a strong focus point of our military support and will continue to be so in the future,” the Netherlands Defense Ministry spokesman Kees Bakhuis told RFE/RL in a written statement on August 6.

Poland's Defense Ministry said all support requests from Ukraine are reviewed by the Polish Armed Forces and organizational units of the ministry as part of the country's comprehensive support -- from the donation of military equipment, to the training of Ukrainian soldiers, to extensive logistical support and medical support -- to Ukraine's Armed Forces.

RFE/RL asked Ukraine's ambassador to NATO, Alyona Hetmanchuk, about the state of negotiations with partner countries, but her response was not available as of publication.

By RFE/RL

title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to Sign Defense Deal
author: Charles Kennedy
excerpt: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey are expected to sign on Friday a joint defense cooperation agreement amid the Middle East’s turmoil triggered by the war in Iran, Reuters reports, citing sources familiar with the plans. On Friday, Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan arrived in Jeddah for an of
content:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey are expected to sign on Friday a joint defense cooperation agreement amid the Middle East’s turmoil triggered by the war in Iran, Reuters reports, citing sources familiar with the plans.

On Friday, Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan arrived in Jeddah for an official visit, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

It wasn’t immediately clear what the commitments of each of the three countries will be in the joint agreement. The three mostly Sunni Muslim powers have been concerned over the turmoil in the Middle East due to the U.S.-Israel war with predominantly Shiite Muslim Iran.

Saudi Arabia is the world’s largest crude oil exporter, Turkey has the biggest NATO army behind the U.S., while Pakistan is a nuclear-armed nation, the only Muslim country to have nuclear weapons.

The war in the Middle East is creating alliances in the region as countries look to protect themselves from attacks and enlist powerful allies to counter threats.

Pakistan has tried to mediate in the U.S.-Iran talks while negotiating with Iran passage of energy commodity cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz, which remains mostly closed with traffic subdued more than five months after the war began on February 28.

Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has declined this week from the prior week amid uncertainty about the U.S.-Iran talks and the potential reopening of the Middle East’s key oil and LNG chokepoint.

Only six crude oil tankers have managed to clear the Strait of Hormuz outbound so far this week, according to Kpler’s ship-tracking data cited by Reuters.

Vessel traffic at the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait crumbled earlier this week amid a Houthi claim they had hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea and hopes that Oman and Iran could reach a deal on jointly managing Hormuz.

Iran on Thursday signaled a much more restrictive regime for vessel traffic than thought, with proposals under review at its parliament to ban U.S. and Israeli ships from transiting the Strait, while other nations that Tehran deems have harmed it would pay compensation for moving through Hormuz.

By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com
